clue.text: It's uncool when rowdy steals a kiss

indicators.note: to steal is to take something in, so the jumble takes the single letter into itself
something rowdy is disorderly, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone thinks snatching a kiss is uncool when the other person is being rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine letters of the first two words are jumbled with A taken in to give OSCULATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Osculation is the formal, rather pompous word for the act of kissing.

clue.text: Like fast food? Perhaps given porridge to eat at first riles one

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece swallows the following letters

parts.note: porridge and stir are both slang for time in prison
one who is fed is given food, hence 'perhaps'

indicators.note: at first points to the very beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of riles
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A prisoner fed porridge gets annoyed by the first spoonful.
explanation.walkthrough: STIR is followed by FED, which takes in R and I: STIR + F(RI)ED. 'Porridge' is British slang for a prison sentence, from the sitcom of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir-fried food is cooked quickly over high heat, so it is literally fast-cooked food; the question mark flags the pun on fast food.

clue.text: Fly out of bounds, doomed

indicators.note: the bounds of a word are its edges, so going out of them strips the first and last letters

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or knowing

explanation.surface: A ball hit out of bounds in some game means the player is doomed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb about a ball; it is the adjective meaning streetwise. KNOWING loses K and G.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-win situation is one that cannot end well whatever you do, so it is doomed.

clue.text: Bolt, not wanting to do qualifiers, forfeits

indicators.note: not wanting something means going without it, so a word meaning to do an impression is dropped

parts.note: to bolt is to escape
to do someone is to impersonate them, to ape them
heats are qualifying races

explanation.surface: Usain Bolt skips the qualifying heats and forfeits his place in the final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bolt' summons the sprinter, whose qualifying races are heats; but it is also the verb meaning escape. ESCAPE minus APE leaves ESC, then HEATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Escheats are properties that revert to the state or crown when there is no heir, so they are forfeits in a legal sense.

clue.text: Target of Harry F remains here

wordplay.note: Tom Brown was the target of the bully Harry Flashman

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry has a target and something remains there.
explanation.walkthrough: In Tom Brown's Schooldays the bully Harry Flashman torments Tom Brown; the clue abbreviates Flashman to F, so the victim is abbreviated to Tom B.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomb is a burial place, the spot where a person's mortal remains lie.

clue.text: Start working with film crew, maybe …

parts.note: a machine that is working is on
a film crew works on the set, and a crew is a set of people

explanation.surface: Someone begins a job working alongside a film crew, the ellipsis carrying the thought into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is the beginning of something, so it is a synonym of start as a noun.

clue.text: Out of it you may get short of light

definitions.text: Out of it you may get short
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the bar device that measures out spirits, a 'short' being a measure of spirits
second meaning: an adjective for things relating to light or vision

explanation.walkthrough: 'Short of light' looks like a phrase about dimness; split after 'short'. In British pubs an optic is the upturned-bottle dispenser, and a short is a single measure of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic names both the pub spirit dispenser and the adjective describing anything relating to light or sight.

clue.text: Assembled a collection of old books about cult object

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the joined letters run backwards

parts.note: people who assembled met
the Old Testament is a collection of old books

explanation.surface: Someone gathers ancient books concerning an object worshipped by a cult.
explanation.walkthrough: METOT read backwards gives TOTEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an emblem, often an animal or carved pole, revered as sacred by a clan or group.

clue.text: … unnecessarily, as Countdown is finally going

parts.note: where a countdown ends up going
a countdown ends at zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Continuing 6 across, someone starts on the set of the TV quiz Countdown, which is ending.
explanation.walkthrough: A countdown finally goes TO O, nought. Countdown is also a long-running British TV word and numbers quiz, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Too means excessively, more than is needed, so it carries the sense of unnecessarily.

clue.text: Could this be Jade Jagger?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: jade is a precious ...
second meaning: Mick Jagger is a Rolling ...

explanation.walkthrough: Jade Jagger is a real person, Mick Jagger's daughter, so the clue looks like a question about her; split the name in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Jade is a green gemstone, and Jagger fronts the Rolling Stones, making him a Stone.

clue.text: Last at 'Aydock OK?

parts.note: the last part is the end
Haydock is a racecourse, home of the horse, and dropping its H as 'Aydock does leaves 'orse

explanation.surface: A racegoer at Haydock asks whether finishing last is all right.
explanation.walkthrough: Haydock Park is an English racecourse; the apostrophe tells you to drop the H the same way, so the animal there is an 'orse.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse something is to approve or sanction it, to say it is OK.

clue.text: Potato cakes a local one scoffs

indicators.note: to cake something is to encase or coat it, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: tater is informal for potato
'un is how a local dialect says one

explanation.surface: Potato cakes are something a local person scoffs, that is, eats greedily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffs' looks like eating to go with the potato cakes; here it means mocks. Tater is informal, chiefly American and dialect, for potato, and 'un is rural speech for one.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff is to jeer or mock, and a person who jeers is a taunter.

clue.text: Horse I see, and a nearly dead man astride it?

definitions.text: Horse I see, and a nearly dead man astride it?

indicators.note: sitting astride means one leg on each side, so letters sit either side of the horse
nearly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: I plus C, the letter that sounds like see
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H
taken as written
a dead man is a body

explanation.surface: Someone spots a horse ridden by a man who looks half dead.
explanation.walkthrough: The horse letter goes in the middle with the other pieces on either side, as a rider sits. The whole clue also describes Ichabod Crane of Washington Irving's Legend of Sleepy Hollow, fleeing the Headless Horseman.
explanation.definitionFit: Ichabod Crane is the terrified schoolmaster who rides away from the Headless Horseman, barely escaping with his life.

clue.text: Spooner's legitimate highland blade

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was famed for swapping the opening sounds of two words

parts.note: to legitimate is to make lawful, to make law; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: Spooner owns a genuine Scottish sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legitimate' looks like an adjective describing the blade; it is the verb, to make law. Swapping M and the K sound gives 'clay more'.
explanation.definitionFit: A claymore is the large two-handed broadsword of the Scottish Highlanders.

clue.text: Caught warning signal: good for driver if it's adverse ahead

definitions.text: good for driver if it's adverse ahead

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the amber traffic light warns drivers to stop

explanation.surface: A driver caught by an amber light, with a road sign warning of trouble ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: British road signs warn of 'adverse camber' where a bend slopes the wrong way; knowing about it in advance helps the driver.
explanation.definitionFit: Camber is the sideways slope of a road; a warning of adverse camber, one tilted the wrong way, is useful to drivers.

clue.text: Rivers' "Spanners" with abstracted depth for pop art

indicators.note: abstracted means taken away, and 'for' says what replaces the removed abbreviation

parts.note: bridges are what span rivers
D is the abbreviation for depth
pop is fizzy drink, such as cola

explanation.surface: Someone's 'Spanners' series of pop art, with its depth taken away, sounds like a gallery review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop art' looks like one phrase but 'pop' is the drink and 'art' alone is the definition. BRIDGES swaps its D for COLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Bricolage is art built from whatever materials come to hand, so bricolages are works of art.

clue.text: Inside of freshwater fish eggs glow

indicators.note: placing something inside another means it is enclosed by it

parts.note: the luce is an old name for the pike, a freshwater fish
eggs is old military slang for mines or bombs

explanation.surface: The insides of river fish have glowing eggs, as if describing a curiosity of nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eggs' wants to be fish roe; it is wartime slang for mines or bombs. The luce is an old name for the pike.
explanation.definitionFit: To luminesce is to emit light without heat, so it is to glow.

clue.text: Sad Menuhin resigns after prelude to botched tune

indicators.note: sad in the sense of sorry or wretched, so the letters are in a sorry state
a prelude comes first, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of botched
taken as written

explanation.surface: The violinist Yehudi Menuhin, unhappy, quits after a botched opening to a piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sad' looks like a description of the violinist but signals the jumble. Bring Me Sunshine was the signature tune of the British comedy duo Morecambe and Wise.
explanation.definitionFit: Bring Me Sunshine is a 1960s song, best known as Morecambe and Wise's closing number, so it is a tune.

clue.text: Soup initiatives for starving children put around pound bags

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it inside a sack, so one piece holds the other
putting something around turns it to face the other way

parts.note: to pound, like a heart, is to throb

indicators.note: initiatives here punningly means initials, the opening letters of the next words

parts.note: the first letters of starving and children

explanation.surface: Charity initiatives give soup to starving children, paid for with money in bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money, the sterling unit; it is the verb, to beat. THROB reversed is BORHT, which bags SC.
explanation.definitionFit: Borscht is the beetroot soup of Eastern Europe.

clue.text: Batting gets worse, and run out is a disaster

indicators.note: batting suggests batty, crazy, or knocked about, so the letters are thrown around
run out in cricket means dismissed, so the run abbreviation is sent away

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A cricket team's batting deteriorates, and a run-out proves disastrous.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface leads to reading 'run out' as a dismissal; instead R leaves GETS WORSE and the rest is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To go west is an idiom for failing, being lost or dying, so something that goes west is a disaster.

clue.text: It's imported by "doppelganger" in German

indicators.note: something imported is brought inside, so the word sits within the following text

parts.note: spans the end of doppelganger, the word in, and the start of German

explanation.surface: A word that English imported from German, doppelganger, being discussed by a language buff.
explanation.walkthrough: Doppelganger is itself a German import, which is the surface's joke; the word also serves as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringer, as in a dead ringer, is someone who looks exactly like another, which is what a doppelganger is.

clue.text: Behold engraver's primary filling so intricately lined?

definitions.text: Behold engraver's primary filling so intricately lined?

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so these letters go in the middle
intricately means in a complicated way, so the letters are tangled
primary means first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of engraver
taken as written
lo is an old word meaning behold

explanation.surface: Look at the engraver's main filler, used for such intricate line work.
explanation.walkthrough: LO and E fill a jumble of LINED. The whole clue also describes the craft: engraved lines are filled with a black alloy.
explanation.definitionFit: Niello is a black metallic alloy inlaid into engraved lines on silver, so a nielloed object has filled, intricately engraved lines.

clue.text: Dictated northern city guides

indicators.note: something dictated is spoken for someone else to write, so we go by sound

parts.note: Leeds is a city in the north of England

explanation.surface: A northern city's guides were dictated to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead someone is to guide them, so leads and guides are synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: One part of me subconsciously turns on another man

indicators.note: something that turns faces the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: in Freud the id is the unconscious part of the psyche
the ego is another of Freud's parts of the self

explanation.surface: Part of someone's subconscious turns against another part, like a psychological drama.
explanation.walkthrough: ID reversed gives DI, followed by EGO; this is a down clue, so 'on' means placed below.
explanation.definitionFit: Diego is a common Spanish man's name, as in Diego Maradona.

clue.text: Suggesting a chicken pasty

parts.note: as, in the sense of like, suggests a likeness
a hen is a chicken

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a chicken pasty, the baked pastry, is on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' looks like the pastry with a chicken filling; it is the adjective meaning pale.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen means pale grey like ash, and a pasty face is pale and unhealthy-looking.

clue.text: Ham slices with dips in a source of magic for kids

definitions.text: a source of magic for kids

indicators.note: dipping in means going inside, so the single letter is placed within
ham acting is overdone and clumsy, so the letters are mangled

parts.note: taken as written
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Ham slices with dips sound like a children's party snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' looks like the meat; it signals a jumble of SLICES with W dipped in.
explanation.definitionFit: C S Lewis wrote the Narnia books, a world of magic for young readers.

clue.text: Basic covering zips up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: zip means nothing, and two zips are O and NIL

explanation.surface: A basic covering, perhaps a jacket, zips up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zips' looks like fastening a jacket; here it is plural zero. O and NIL read upwards give LINO.
explanation.definitionFit: Lino, short for linoleum, is a cheap, plain floor covering.

clue.text: Articulated parts of Glasgow-Edinburgh link give out

indicators.note: articulated means spoken clearly, so we go by the sound

parts.note: the M8 motorway links Glasgow and Edinburgh; its parts are M and 8

explanation.surface: Sections of the road between Glasgow and Edinburgh are articulated, like lorries, and give out.
explanation.walkthrough: The M8 is the Scottish motorway joining the two cities; say its parts as 'M and 8' casually.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or flow out from a source, so it means to give out.

clue.text: Hats off to our new editor scrutinising styles

indicators.note: hats sit on top of heads, so only the heads of these words are kept

parts.note: the first letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: Congratulations to the paper's new editor, who will examine house styles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hats off to' looks like praise; the hats are the initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tones in the sense of manners or registers of expression are styles.

clue.text: More of which you can guess we tick at prime locations

definitions.text: More of which you can guess

indicators.note: prime locations are the prime-numbered positions, second, third and fifth

parts.note: letters two, three and five

explanation.surface: Estate agents tick boxes at prime locations, and you can guess the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime locations' sounds like estate-agent talk; it means letters at prime-number positions.
explanation.definitionFit: Etc, short for et cetera, means 'and the rest', implying more of the same that the reader can supply.

clue.text: Tips on shorthand typing I'll return?

definitions.text: Tips on shorthand typing I'll return?

indicators.note: the tips of words are their ends, here the leading letters

parts.note: the first letters of shorthand and typing

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A stenographer promises to come back with advice about shorthand typing.
explanation.walkthrough: ST followed by ONE reversed. The whole clue also hints at a steno, someone who returns typed shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: Steno is short for stenography or stenographer, the craft or practitioner of shorthand typing.
